I agree with /u/aatmkaa about needing his polarity to offset the other extreme, but where I disagree with Stallman is in his belief that proprietary software has absolutely 0 place in the world. I think the GPL has a place just as much as the MIT/BSD licenses have a place. Sometimes a proprietary license is the right one. Stallman is too steadfast in his need for purity.

Stallman also acts as the beacon for anyone privacy-conscious. I worry who will pick up his torch when he goes, but right now he is the sole-truth for anyone needing a guiding light or something to aspire to w.r.t. privacy both digital and real-world.

What Stallman proposes is the utopian ideal. Pragmatism requires trading some of the freedom that he insists upon for the ability to interact with others. There's enough proprietary de facto standards out there that a 100% free OS running 100% free software would not be very useful. It requires cooperation from others that you have no control over, e.g. if your boss sends you an Excel file, you can't well expect to keep your job if you kick it back to him and tell him that you can't open it and to please send in an opendoc format.

I think it's very good he exists and I think it's good that he espouses his ideals so loudly.
I think you underestimate the state of free software. You can easily run a 100% free OS and userland that is very useful (and, yes, can open Excel files).

I respect him very much and his ideals. I think he is right that if you sell something, you should also include the source code or at least make it available, so that you can be sure that it does not funny things on your machine.

Of course, people and companies need to get paid for their work. But as a user, I should decide what my machine is doing. For example, think about some vulnerability in a software, for examples sake take windows xp. Somebody programmed in vb 6 some application for a little company, and it works like a charme, but Windows XP is not supported anymore. If some vulnerability is found in XP, that affects this application, the company can't do much, they need to move to another os and pay someone to port their software. If it was open source, some people could close the vulnerability voluntarily. Now lets say, this company was really big, it is an enterprise, but they are also using XP. They whole infrastructure depends on it. And the vuln. is really new. The enterprise really wants to close this vuln. else it would be really expensive. So if it was open source, they could pay some expert to close it.

And btw. he does not want that every software should be made public. And some people are afraid, that if the source is published, someone else can copy it. No, if every software was open source, you can use simple tools like they use for academia, to find these copied pieces.

Stallman is GNU-SLASH-LINUX's Jesus. He teaches us the path to true FLOSS (or "unfettered software") heaven. He is consistent and unquestioningly right. Most importantly he practices what he preaches. He is the example that we should all strive to. However he is also probably at least partly crazy, entirely impractical, eccentric and quite honestly awesome.

Linus is pragmatic. While the GNU project was dreaming big with HURD, Linus made the practical and simple Linux kernel. He tempts us with blobs and flips off GPU companies.In order to actually do anything productive in GNU-SLASH-LINUX we need to be like Linus. But we should all strive to be like Stallman.

Stallman saves.
